content.paragraph: The formulas of this section enable us to differentiate new functions that are formed from old functions by using multiplication or division.

subsection.title: The Product Rule
subsection.paragraph: By analogy with the Sum and Difference Rules, we might be tempted to guess, as Leibniz did three centuries ago, that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives. We can see, however, that this guess is wrong by looking at a particular example. Let $$f(x) = x$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ . Then the Power Rule gives $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1$$ and $$g^{\prime}(x) = 2x$$ . But $$\left( {fg} \right)(x) = x^{3}$$ , so $$\left( {fg} \right)^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ . Thus $$\left( {fg} \right)^{\prime} \neq f^{\prime}g^{\prime}$$ . The correct formula was discovered by Leibniz (soon after his false start) and is called the Product Rule.

Before stating the Product Rule, let’s see how we might discover it. We start by assuming that $$u = f(x)$$ and $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ are both positive differentiable functions. Then we can interpret the product $$u\upsilon$$ as an area of a rectangle (see Figure 1). If $$x$$ changes by an amount $$\Delta x$$ , then the corresponding changes in $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are

paragraph.math: $${\Delta u = f\left( {x + \Delta x} \right) - f(x)\qquad}{\Delta\upsilon = g\left( {x + \Delta x} \right) - g(x)}$$

subsection.paragraph: and the new value of the product, $$\left( {u + \Delta u} \right)\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)$$ , can be interpreted as the area of the large rectangle in Figure 1 (provided that $$\Delta u$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ happen to be positive).

If we divide by $$\Delta x$$ , we get

paragraph.math: $$\frac{\Delta\left( {u\upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}$$

subsection.paragraph: If we now let $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we get the derivative of $$u\upsilon$$ :

paragraph.math: $$= {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\left( {u\upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\left( {u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}} \right)}$$

$$= {u\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \left( {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\Delta u} \right)\left( {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}} \right)}$$

subsection.paragraph: (Notice that $$\left. \Delta u\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ since $$f$$ is differentiable and therefore continuous.)

Although we started by assuming (for the geometric interpretation) that all the quantities are positive, we notice that Equation 1 is always true. (The algebra is valid whether $$u$$ , $$\upsilon$$ , $$\Delta u$$ , and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ are positive or negative.) So we have proved Equation 2, known as the Product Rule, for all differentiable functions $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ .

subsection.title: The Quotient Rule
subsection.paragraph: We find a rule for differentiating the quotient of two differentiable functions $$u = f(x)$$ and $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ in much the same way that we found the Product Rule. If $$x$$ , $$u$$ , and $$\upsilon$$ change by amounts $$\Delta x$$ , $$\Delta u$$ , and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ , then the corresponding change in the quotient $$u \slash \upsilon$$ is

paragraph.math: $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right) = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\left( {u \slash \upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} - u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}}{\upsilon\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)}$$

subsection.paragraph: As $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , $$\left. \Delta\upsilon\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ also, because $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ is differentiable and therefore continuous. Thus, using the Limit Laws, we get

paragraph.math: $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right) = \frac{\upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} - u\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}}{\upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)} = \frac{\upsilon\frac{du}{\mathit{dx}} - u\frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dx}}}{\upsilon^{2}}$$

subsection.paragraph: In words, the Quotient Rule says that the derivative of a quotient is the denominator times the derivative of the numerator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator, all divided by the square of the denominator.
The Quotient Rule and the other differentiation formulas enable us to compute the derivative of any rational function, as the next example illustrates.
